newsitem.title: FRANCE: French wages must match wealth - white-collar union.
newsitem.headline: French wages must match wealth - white-collar union.

text.p: France's CGC white-collar trade union said on Tuesday that a national conference on jobs, work and wages should lead to an overhaul of wealth distribution and the organisation of work.
CGC union leader Marc Vilbenoit said the left-wing victory in Sunday's parliamentary election had showed that French voters had "shut the door on the shift towards ultra liberalism".

Wages had suffered for far too long in favour of corporate and capital profit, he told Reuters in a telephone interview. The CGC, one of France's larger unions, represents mainly private sector workers.

The national work, employment and wages conference promised by new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin should produce genuine reforms to allow wage-earners and consumers to share more equally in increasing national wealth, he said.

"If you look two decades ahead, we will have a population which remains the same and a doubling of wealth. The way in which wealth is tapped (by government) has to change so that it is not wages alone which carry the burden," Vilbenoit said.
"Wages have retreated in terms of national wealth for the past 15 years," he said.
The CGC is one of a number of unions to spell out its demands as a new Socialist-led government prepared to take power from the centre-right coalition, which was beaten on Sunday.
The CGC's top priority at the conference of social partners would be opening a "genuine discussion on the sharing of productivity gains in the long term", said Vilbenoit.
"We should be able to develop some form of mechanism...which would adjust the balance between wages, capital income, jobs and work time," he said.
Jospin has not yet set a date for the conference, although it is expected by the summer.

Globalisation, increasing international competition and a "second industrial revolution" in technology would produce a more productive economy, but one in which the whole organisation of work needed to be reformulated.

"First time round there was the invention of paid holidays, then there was the invention of work training. Now we need to invent a whole new way of capitalising career lives, with time for the family, time to return to studies," Vilbenoit said.
"We will present proposals on upgrading salaries, on the negotiation of pay scales and on pushing for a reduction in working time based on new forms of work reorganisation."
The Socialist party plans to get employers and unions together at the conference and has also set a goal of reducing the work week to 35 hours from 39 within three years.
Vilbenoit said his union wanted a reduction of work time but not as a uniform measure.
Wages would have to benefit after years of bearing the brunt of charges imposed by successive governments to support the social security system and the national budget, he said.
"The civil service has fallen behind but I can assure you that the story is just the same in the private sector," he said. His union has not formulated a wage demand in terms of figures.
Vilbenoit said the CGC was not opposed to privatisations in sectors such as rail or power utilities. It favours privatisation of France Telecom.
The future of plans to sell a stake in the state telecoms operator is unclear after the centre-right's defeat and before a decision is taken by the incoming Socialist government.

The CGC favours a rise in the national minimum wage beyond the indexed increase every July. Vilbenoit said he would like to see the minimum raised by that date but the increase should not be "to the detriment of employment".

French unemployment is running at a post-war record 12.8 percent with more than three million official jobseekers and is seen as one of the main reasons for a swing to the left in the parliamentary election.
-- Brian Love, Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452
